title: Low blood sugar after insulin
objectives: Recognize and treat hypoglycemia following an insulin dose
Follow the treat-then-recheck sequence rather than a single blind treatment
Document a medication-related event with the full timeline of treatment and recheck
opening: You gave Mr. Kim his scheduled sliding-scale lispro at 1130 based on a fingerstick of 240, then went to your next patient. Forty-five minutes later, his call light goes on. You find him diaphoretic, shaky, and saying he feels 'off' and lightheaded. His lunch tray is untouched on the table.

actions.label: Recheck his blood glucose immediately
actions.response: Fingerstick reads 52 mg/dL. He is diaphoretic, tremulous, and able to answer questions appropriately — alert and able to swallow safely.
actions.criticalWhy: Confirming the number before treating avoids both under- and over-treating, and tells you whether he can safely take something by mouth.

actions.label: Give his next scheduled insulin dose since it's near mealtime
actions.detail: It's almost time for lunch coverage anyway.
actions.response: Giving insulin to a patient who is already hypoglycemic would worsen a dangerous situation. Any scheduled insulin is held until this episode is treated and resolved — this is exactly the kind of order you'd question rather than follow automatically.

actions.label: Give 15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
actions.detail: He is alert and able to swallow safely.
actions.response: He drinks 4 oz of juice from his tray. Reports feeling slightly less shaky already but still lightheaded.

actions.label: Assume the juice fixed it and move on to your next task
actions.detail: He said he feels a little better.
actions.response: Feeling subjectively better is not the same as a confirmed number. The standard is to recheck in 15 minutes and treat again if still low — moving on without that recheck risks missing a persistent or rebounding low.

actions.label: Recheck his blood glucose after 15 minutes
actions.detail: Confirm the treatment worked before clearing him.
actions.response: Fingerstick now reads 78 mg/dL. He states he feels much better, tremors resolved. Still below target range for a stable reading.

actions.label: Give another 15 g of carbohydrate since it's still under 80
actions.detail: Standard is to repeat if still below target.
actions.response: He eats crackers from his tray. Tolerates well, no nausea.

actions.label: Notify the provider of the hypoglycemic episode
actions.detail: Report the value, treatment given, and current status.
actions.response: Dr. Alvarez is notified. New order: recheck fingerstick before dinner dose, hold the next sliding-scale dose if under 100, and reduce tonight's glargine to 16 units given the trend.

actions.label: Encourage him to eat his lunch tray now
actions.detail: A sustained source, not just simple sugar.
actions.response: He eats roughly 75% of his tray, including protein and starch. States he feels back to normal.

actions.label: Recheck blood glucose one more time before charting the episode closed
actions.detail: Confirm a stable, safe number before considering this resolved.
actions.response: Fingerstick reads 118 mg/dL. Stable, no further symptoms. He is resting comfortably.

hints: The first step is always to confirm the number, not to treat off of how he looks.
One round of carbohydrate and one recheck is often not enough — check the trend.
A number back in range doesn't mean the shift's job here is done — the provider still needs this for tonight's orders.

documentation.prompt: Write your nursing note covering the episode from recognition through resolution.
documentation.placeholder: Begin with the time and what prompted you to check...

requirements.label: Symptoms and initial glucose value that prompted treatment
requirements.why: Establishes this was a real, confirmed low, not a guess.

requirements.label: First treatment given, with amount and time
requirements.why: The 15-15 rule only works if the dose and timing are documented, not just 'treated.'

requirements.label: First recheck value after treatment
requirements.why: Shows the treatment was verified, not assumed to have worked.

requirements.label: Second round of treatment, since the recheck was still low
requirements.why: Shows the protocol was followed through to an actual resolution, not stopped after one round.

requirements.label: Final glucose value confirming resolution
requirements.why: The episode isn't closed in the note until a stable number is documented.

requirements.label: Provider notified, with time and new orders
requirements.why: This event needs to change tonight's insulin plan, not repeat itself.

requirements.label: Scheduled insulin held or adjusted as a result
requirements.why: Documents the safety action taken, not just the recovery.

documentation.modelNote:
1216 — Called to room by call light. Patient found diaphoretic, tremulous, reporting feeling 'off' and lightheaded, lunch tray untouched. Received scheduled sliding-scale lispro at 1130 per fingerstick of 240. Fingerstick rechecked immediately: 52 mg/dL. Patient alert, able to swallow safely.

1217 — 4 oz juice (approx. 15 g carbohydrate) given per hypoglycemia protocol. Patient reports feeling slightly improved but still lightheaded.

1231 — Fingerstick rechecked: 78 mg/dL. Tremors resolved but still below target. Additional 15 g carbohydrate (crackers) given, tolerated without nausea.

1235 — Dr. Alvarez notified of hypoglycemic episode, treatment given, and current trend. New orders: recheck fingerstick before dinner dose, hold next sliding-scale dose if under 100, reduce tonight's glargine to 16 units.

1238 — Patient encouraged to eat remainder of lunch tray for sustained glucose source; consumed approximately 75% including protein and starch.

1246 — Final fingerstick recheck: 118 mg/dL, stable. Patient reports feeling back to normal, resting comfortably, no further symptoms. Will continue to monitor per new orders.
pitfalls: Charting 'treated for low blood sugar' without the actual glucose number.
Stopping after one recheck instead of following through to a stable, resolved value.
Forgetting to note that the scheduled insulin dose was held, not just that the low was treated.
Leaving out the time the provider was notified — this event changes tonight's orders.
